headings.title: Introduction to Maternal Nutrition and Physiology
headings.content: Pregnancy brings major changes to a woman's body. Blood volume increases by up to fifty percent to supply the growing placenta and fetus. To support this, the body absorbs nutrients much more efficiently from the food a pregnant mother eats. Metabolic demands rise steadily, especially during the second and third trimesters. Nursing assessment must account for these normal physiological shifts rather than mistaking them for pathology.

headings.title: Macronutrient Requirements in Pregnancy
headings.content: Expectant mothers need more energy and building blocks than usual, but the old saying about eating for two is misleading. Caloric needs rise only slightly in the first trimester, adding about three hundred extra calories per day in the later stages. Protein intake must increase to support the growth of uterine tissue, breast tissue, and the baby itself. Carbohydrates provide the primary fuel for fetal brain development, while healthy fats support cell membrane formation.

headings.title: Essential Micronutrients: Iron, Calcium, and Folate
headings.content:
Specific vitamins and minerals play critical roles in preventing birth defects and maternal illness. 

- **Folate (Folic Acid)**: Prevents neural tube defects and should ideally be started before conception.
- **Iron**: Supports the massive expansion of red blood cells and prevents maternal anemia.
- **Calcium**: Protects maternal bone density while building the fetal skeleton.

headings.title: Fluid Balance and Hydration Needs
headings.content: Water is a vital nutrient that is frequently overlooked in prenatal counseling. Increased blood volume, amniotic fluid, and higher metabolic waste elimination mean fluid needs rise significantly. Dehydration can trigger uterine irritability, headaches, and premature contractions. Encouraging adequate water consumption throughout the day helps prevent urinary tract infections, which are common during pregnancy.

headings.title: Nutritional Assessment and Dietary Planning
headings.content: Every prenatal visit should include a basic nutritional check. Nurses assess pre-pregnancy weight, current weight gain patterns, and dietary habits. A sudden, excessive weight gain can signal gestational hypertension or fluid retention, while poor weight gain may indicate fetal growth restriction. Dietary plans must respect local food availability, household finances, and personal preferences to be realistic.

headings.title: Managing Pregnancy-Related Dietary Discomforts
headings.content: Common discomforts like nausea, heartburn, and constipation can severely disrupt a healthy diet. Morning sickness often responds well to eating small, dry carbohydrate snacks before getting out of bed. Heartburn can be minimized by avoiding spicy foods and remaining upright after eating. Constipation, worsened by sluggish bowels from progesterone, requires adequate fiber and increased fluid intake.

headings.title: Cultural Dietary Practices and Nursing Counseling in Nigeria
headings.content: Nutritional counseling must respect local Nigerian food traditions while correcting harmful myths. Some cultural practices encourage nourishing porridges like pap enriched with groundnut paste, while others mistakenly restrict nutritious foods like eggs or meat during pregnancy. Nurses must listen respectfully, identify valuable local staples such as beans, plantains, and dark leafy greens, and guide mothers toward balanced, safe choices without causing offense.
